summaries.example: Imagine this argument: If the school bus is late, Maya will miss the first bell. The bus is late. So Maya will miss the first bell. If both starting statements are true, the last statement must be true too. That is a deductively valid argument. But an argument about swans is different: all swans we have seen are white, so the next swan must be white. That conclusion might be wrong, because the next swan could be black.
summaries.summary: Logical consequence is the special relationship in which a conclusion follows from premises. In deductive logic, the relationship is meant to be exceptionless: if the premises are all true, the conclusion cannot be false. This does not by itself make the premises true. Inductive reasoning is different. It uses evidence to make a conclusion more likely, but the conclusion may still fail. Philosophers also separate material consequence, which depends on the meanings and facts in a particular argument, from formal consequence, which depends on logical structure. For example, a family relationship may let us move from one claim to another, but that step uses the meanings of “mother,” “brother,” and “cousin.” Modern logic studies consequence with models and proofs. A model can show that an argument fails by giving a case where the premises are true and the conclusion is false. A proof uses small rule-governed steps to establish the conclusion. In many important systems, models and proofs agree about which arguments are valid, though they explain validity in different ways. The entry also discusses different numbers of premises and conclusions, special systems that reject some usual rules for combining premises, and the debate over whether there is one logical consequence relation or several.
key_ideas: Logic studies when a conclusion really follows from premises.
Deductive arguments aim at certainty; inductive arguments make a conclusion more likely but can still be wrong.
A valid argument can have a false conclusion if one or more premises are false.
Formal consequence depends on the shape of an argument rather than the special facts in its words.
Models look for possible counterexamples, while proofs show a route from premises to conclusion.
Different logicians disagree about whether there is one kind of logical consequence or several.
summaries.why_it_matters: Logical consequence helps us tell the difference between a strong reason and a guess. It is useful in mathematics, computer science, careful conversation, and everyday decisions. Learning it also teaches an important habit: check both the reasons and the connection between the reasons and the conclusion.

important_terms.definition: A starting statement in an argument. Premises are offered as reasons for a conclusion.
The statement an argument tries to support or show.
An argument is deductively valid when true premises cannot go together with a false conclusion.
A way that one statement follows from others because of their pattern or structure, not their special topic.
A possible arrangement or interpretation used to test whether an argument has a counterexample.
A step-by-step way to get a conclusion from premises by using accepted rules.

questions_to_think_about: Can an argument be valid even when its conclusion is false?
Why is “all swans seen so far were white” not enough to guarantee that every swan is white?
Would you rather test an argument by looking for a counterexample or by building a proof? Why?
Could the same argument be judged differently in different kinds of logic?

summaries.example: Consider: “Every registered bird in the survey has a tag. Kiko is a registered bird in the survey. Therefore, Kiko has a tag.” The argument is formally valid because its pattern guarantees the conclusion whenever the premises are true. By contrast, “Every bird observed this month has been a crow; therefore, the next bird observed will be a crow” is inductive. Its evidence may make the conclusion reasonable, but it does not rule out an exception. A model-theoretic test searches for an interpretation in which the premises are true and the conclusion false; if one exists, the argument is not valid.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what it means for a conclusion to follow from premises. Deductive consequence is usually characterized as necessary truth preservation: there is no acceptable case in which all premises are true and the conclusion false. This differs from inductive consequence, where premises raise the probability or reasonableness of a conclusion without guaranteeing it. The notion of necessity itself is disputed. Metaphysical necessity can include truths whose status depends on how the world is, such as the identity of water with H2O, while logical consequence is generally expected to be available without empirical discovery. Conceptual, analytic, and a priori necessity each capture some features but face difficulties. A further central requirement is formality. Logical consequence should not depend on the topic-specific content of an argument, but philosophers disagree about how to identify logical form and logical vocabulary. Model theory treats validity as truth preservation across models, with a countermodel serving as a failure case. Proof theory treats validity as the existence of a derivation built from inference rules, emphasizing how a conclusion can be established and how rules may determine meaning. Neither approach is simply free of philosophical challenges. Questions arise about what models represent, which expressions count as logical, and which inference rules genuinely determine meaning. Soundness and completeness theorems often connect the two approaches. The entry further considers single and multiple conclusions, structural rules challenged by relevant and substructural logics, and the possibility that “logical consequence” names a family of related notions rather than one universally fixed relation.
key_ideas: Deductive validity requires necessary truth preservation, whereas inductive support concerns probability or reasonableness.
Metaphysical necessity alone may be too broad for logical consequence: necessary truths discovered through experience need not be logical truths.
Formality is difficult to define; proposals include generality, invariance under permutations, abstraction from content, and rules applying to thought regardless of topic.
Model theory defines validity through the absence of a countermodel, while proof theory defines it through derivability by accepted inference rules.
Soundness and completeness can show that a proof system and a model-theoretic semantics agree in extension, even if they offer different philosophical explanations.
Logical monism, contextualism, and pluralism disagree about whether validity is one relation, context-dependent, or sometimes best described in more than one way.
summaries.why_it_matters: The concept of logical consequence underlies proof, explanation, mathematics, formal semantics, and debates about rational belief. It clarifies why a true conclusion is not enough for a good argument: the route from premises must also be appropriate. Comparing models and proofs also reveals a broader philosophical issue—whether logic is fundamentally about truth, structure, meaning, or the methods by which thinkers obtain justification.

important_terms.definition: A relation in which the truth of the premises guarantees the truth of the conclusion in the relevant, exceptionless sense.
Validity understood as preservation of truth by necessity, rather than merely making a conclusion probable.
A consequence that depends on particular meanings or facts, rather than only on logical structure.
A consequence grounded in the form of an argument and intended to be neutral about its subject matter.
A mathematical structure that assigns interpretations to expressions and is used to test truth and validity.
A rule-governed sequence of inferences from premises to a conclusion.
A proof system is sound when everything it proves is valid under the chosen semantics.
A proof system is complete when every argument valid under the chosen semantics can be proved in that system.

questions_to_think_about: Why might the necessary truth of “water is H2O” fail to make the inference from “x is water” to “x is H2O” a logical inference?
Is a family-based inference formal, material, or dependent on how “formal” is defined?
Does a countermodel explain validity better than a proof, or do the two approaches answer different questions?
Should adding an unused premise preserve validity?
Can two logical systems reasonably assign different statuses to the same argument?

summaries.example: Suppose a club says: “If a member returns a library book late, the member pays a fine. Jordan returned a book late. So Jordan pays a fine.” The conclusion follows if the club’s rule and the second statement are true. Now compare: “The last ten buses arrived on time, so the next bus will arrive on time.” This is an inductive argument. It may be sensible, but traffic or a breakdown could make it wrong. The first argument is about a guaranteed pattern; the second is about evidence and likelihood.
summaries.summary: Logical consequence asks when a conclusion follows from one or more premises. In deductive reasoning, the goal is a guarantee: if all the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false. This is what validity means in the central logical sense. Validity does not say that the premises are actually true. Inductive reasoning has a different goal. Its premises may make a conclusion more likely or more reasonable, but an exception can still occur. The entry then asks what makes deductive following logical. One proposal appeals to necessity, but several kinds of necessity are possible. A statement may be necessarily true because of how the world is, yet discovering it may require science rather than logic. Another proposal appeals to concepts or meanings, but the boundaries between analytic and non-analytic truths are debated. A major proposal says that logical consequence is formal: it depends on the arrangement and role of expressions, not on special facts about the topic. Even this idea needs explanation, because some arguments work only because of meanings such as family relationships. Modern discussions use two main mathematical tools. Model theory describes interpretations in which sentences are true and defines validity by the absence of a case where premises are true and the conclusion false. Proof theory describes derivations made from inference rules. Proofs highlight how a reasoner can move from grounds for premises to grounds for a conclusion. Soundness and completeness results can connect these approaches, though they do not settle every philosophical question. The entry also considers how many premises or conclusions an argument may have, whether some usual rules should be rejected, and whether logical consequence is one relation or a group of related ideas.
key_ideas: A valid argument can start with false premises; validity concerns the connection between premises and conclusion.
Inductive arguments can be strong without being deductively valid because their evidence does not eliminate every possible exception.
Philosophers debate what kind of necessity belongs to logic and how it differs from facts discovered about the world.
Formal logic tries to capture patterns that do not depend on the topic, but deciding what counts as logical form is itself difficult.
Models test arguments by searching for counterexamples; proofs establish arguments through permitted steps.
Some logicians defend one standard of consequence, while others allow context-sensitive or multiple standards.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic gives us a careful way to judge reasoning. It helps explain why a prediction can be well supported without being certain, and why a conclusion can be true for the wrong reasons. It also connects everyday argument with mathematics and computer-based systems that use formal rules.

important_terms.definition: A reason or statement used to support another statement.
The statement an argument attempts to establish.
A property of an argument whose true premises guarantee that its conclusion is true.
Reasoning that aims to make a conclusion certain if the premises are true.
Reasoning that uses evidence to make a conclusion more likely, without guaranteeing it.
Following that depends on the argument’s subject matter or meanings, not just its logical pattern.
Following that depends on logical structure while setting aside particular subject matter.
A mathematical interpretation or situation used to check whether premises can be true while a conclusion is false.

questions_to_think_about: Why does a false premise not automatically make an argument invalid?
What would count as a counterexample to an argument?
Should a rule of logic depend on what an argument is about?
Why might two proof systems agree about valid arguments but explain validity differently?
Is it better to say that there is one logic or that different settings can use different logics?
